claims.text: The material family of interest is multiphase Ni-based superalloys.
The primary mechanical property of interest is tensile ductility, measured through elongation and reduction of area.
The relevant Ni-based superalloys contain high concentrations of refractory elements such as Re and Ru.
The initial alloy contains a gamma matrix and gamma-prime precipitates.
The initial alloy has a high volume fraction of refractory elements Re, Ru, and W.
Aging at intermediate temperatures of 600–800 degrees Celsius will produce a ductile-brittle-ductile transition.
During aging, chemical ordering in the gamma-prime precipitates increases and is subsequently followed by precipitate coarsening.
The minimum in ductility occurs when chemical ordering of the gamma-prime precipitates reaches its maximum.
Gamma-prime precipitates evolve from a disordered or low-order state into highly ordered DO3 or L12 superstructures.
Chemical ordering changes lattice-mismatch strain fields around the gamma-prime precipitates.
Disordered or weakly ordered gamma-prime precipitates permit an initially ductile state.
Increasing chemical order creates strong anti-phase boundaries that impede dislocation motion and cause embrittlement.
Longer aging causes precipitate coarsening that reduces the number density of anti-phase boundaries.
Precipitate coarsening relaxes lattice-mismatch strain.
Reduced anti-phase-boundary density and relaxed mismatch strain restore ductility at long aging times.
Ductility versus aging time follows a U-shaped curve.
Sufficient refractory content is required to stabilize complex ordered phases such as DO3.
The transition requires ordering kinetics to be faster than coarsening kinetics and a temperature below 0.8 times the melting temperature.
Substantial ordering in the initial microstructure may mask the proposed transition.
Topologically close-packed phase formation may dominate failure and mask the proposed transition.

contradictions.description: The initial precipitates are designated gamma-prime, while the mediator and mechanism also describe those gamma-prime precipitates as initially disordered and only later becoming L12 or DO3 ordered. The use of the gamma-prime label for both the purportedly disordered precursor and the ordered product is internally ambiguous.
